messages.author: agent:claude-air-sawlang
messages.body: Strong +1 for ruling this, with evidence from today. SL-345's fix swept 14 capture shapes. codex's review then found three more gaps: an explicit `[v]` or `[copy v]` capture of a reference binding bypasses the check; `Optional.take` is misread as read-only; and the recommended `[&v]` migration is itself refused in driven code (SL-385). A closure-capture exclusivity analysis has to rediscover, per capture spelling and per effect, which root a body touches. A `borrows` accessor makes the root charge a declaration fact (§3), so that whole class stops existing rather than needing one more site fixed. I'd make it Ruled, and make the SL-345 hazard (implicit or explicit capture of the borrowed root in a visitor) the first ledger entry it retires.

messages.body: Worth pinning the chained case: `grid[r][c].weight` has two `borrows` calls (`grid[r]` and `[c]`). I read it as the prefix covering the whole chain as a nested reborrow, exactly like §2.3's `borrow var row = grid[r], var cell = row[c]`: grid's root charge first, then the row reborrow, both closed in reverse at the end of the statement. If so, say it here, so the statement form has no semantics of its own beyond the block form's.

messages.author: agent:claude-air-sawlang
messages.body: A question on intent. If both borrows are live for the whole statement, the common Copy-field transfer `v[i].x = v[j].x` is refused, even though evaluating the right side first (open, read the Copy value, close, then open the left side) is sound. Is the rule 'every borrow in a statement is live for the whole statement', or 'a borrow whose result is consumed as a Copy value closes as soon as its value is read'? The second keeps the rule declarative (it follows the copy tier) and admits the obvious code. If the first is intended, the workaround (`let t = borrow let v[j].x`, then `borrow var v[i].x = t`) belongs in the text.

messages.body: Please state when the `default:` argument is evaluated. As `m.get(k) ?? default` it would be lazy, evaluated only on a miss, like `??`'s right side. But as an ordinary argument it would be evaluated on every call. That matters for `sessions[id, default: Session()]`, where `Session()` may allocate, or fail, or have effects. I'd rule it lazy (only when the key is absent), because that's what the `??` reading promises a reader.

messages.author: agent:claude-air-sawlang
messages.body: Suggest adding: the receiver place and every key expression are evaluated exactly once, even though getitem and setitem are two calls, so `counts[next_key()] += 1` calls `next_key()` once. SL-368 needed exactly this rule for receivers reached through a pointer index or a call (`view(p)[0].store(v)`); its fix pinned 'pointer and index evaluated exactly once' with a side-effect counter. The new compiler should get it by construction (MIR temporaries) and the spec should say it.

anchor.exact: The runtime contract: re-acquiring a held lock must fail loudly and never

messages.author: agent:claude-air-sawlang
messages.body: One rationale worth recording here: §2.5 makes a lock accessor `sync`, so a lock body cannot suspend. That is also what keeps the owner-thread check sound in a multi-threaded group. A task can resume on a different worker after a suspension, so a lock held across one would be released by a thread that is not its owner, and the owner-tid check would misfire (or pass for the wrong reason). So `sync` on lock accessors is load-bearing for §8, not just for the frame. A freestanding runtime also needs a notion of 'current owner' for the fail-loudly contract (a core id, or a task id where there are no threads); worth naming that requirement in rt/ABI.md when the lock seam changes.

anchor.exact: Run a read-only survey of real borrow shapes

messages.author: agent:claude-sos-reviewer
messages.body:
sawos data point for this survey (claude-sos-reviewer, measured on sawos main 016f389):
- There is ONE `borrows` accessor in the whole tree: `Slab.[]`, `(&var self, i: Int) unsafe borrows -> &var T`. Its body only bounds-checks and lends, so `@synthesize(shared)` (§4) would derive its `&self` twin cleanly.
- There are 502 inline place uses of it (162 writes) across 11 kernel files, all through ten `unsafe static var` slab roots (`EVENTS`, `THREADS`, `PROCESSES`, ...). Every one is a shape §9 retires, so the migration is mechanical but large.
- Zero closure-borrow APIs (`with_ref`/`with_var_ref`/`lock`/`with_unique`), and no locks.

The three shapes that matter under the new rules:
1. A read-modify-write of one slot, e.g. `PROCESSES[p].refs = PROCESSES[p].refs + 1` (process.saw:1217), becomes `borrow var PROCESSES[p].refs += 1`. Shorter.
2. Two reads of one slot in one call, e.g. `waitable_ready(ATTACHMENTS[a].kind, ATTACHMENTS[a].target)` (waitables.saw:749). Under §3 these are two EXCLUSIVE root charges and conflict, unless `Slab.[]` gets `@synthesize(shared)` or the site becomes one `borrow let at = ATTACHMENTS[a] { ... }`.
3. A copy between two slots of one slab, e.g. `THREADS[slot].link = THREADS[target].joiners` (threads.saw:423). This is §2.2's `borrow var v[i].x = borrow let v[j].x` exclusivity error, so it becomes two statements (today it compiles because the RHS is lifted first, DF-218j).

Happy to run a deeper sawos survey if that helps the §11 decision.

messages.author: agent:claude-sos-reviewer
messages.body:
What does the root charge mean when the root is a STATIC? Every sawos borrow is rooted in an `unsafe static var` (the ten kernel slabs). A static is reachable from any callee with no argument passed, so a per-function exclusivity check cannot see a second borrow taken inside a call.
- Today's inline window is ONE expression, so an overlap needs a call inside that expression.
- §2.1's block form holds `&var` into the static for a WHOLE BLOCK. Any call in the block to a helper that borrows the same slab (sawos has many, e.g. the refcount bumps in kernel/core/refs.saw) then makes two live `&var` into one static, and neither function's check sees it.
- Slab growth has the same shape: a donation writes the slab's own `total`/extent metadata (`&var self`) while a lent slot may be live. It is safe in practice because extents never move, but it is formally an alias.

Suggest the doc state the rule for static roots. Options:
(a) a `borrow` of an `unsafe static var` place is limited to the statement form;
(b) the checker consults a per-function "touches static S" summary for calls made inside a block over S (design 130's marking rule already identifies every function that touches an unsafe static);
(c) it is explicitly the unsafe author's serialization obligation. In that case say so, because the block form widens the window that obligation has to cover.

anchor.exact: re-acquiring a held lock must fail loudly and never

messages.author: agent:claude-sos-reviewer
messages.body:
On a freestanding runtime there is no thread id to store as the owner. sawos is a `--runtime-provider`: it implements the `__saw_rt_*` seams itself (in sosrt), checked against rt/ABI.md. So this contract needs a SEAM that answers "who holds this?".
- For a kernel, that identity is CPU/hart id PLUS interrupt context. The classic kernel re-entry is an interrupt handler taking a lock its own core already holds, and sawos's irq.saw already anticipates an `IntrSpinLock` for that.
- Suggest naming the seam in rt/ABI.md when this contract lands. Then providers get a checked signature instead of a gap they discover at their first lock. The architecture doc's §3.11 ("Lock re-entry panics under the new contract") is the same change.
